title: The tool-venv bind-mount shadows the env's own checkout and breaks it
description:
Self-inflicted, by the poly-7z1 fix in commit 406c7db. It breaks a
working env.

prepare_root_runtime bind-mounts the host's tool venv read-only at
/work/polytropos. That path is not free: layout.py:41 defines
TOOL_DIR = "/work/polytropos" and documents it as "this tool's own
checkout", exported into every chroot as POLYTROPOS_ROOT, with the
repository's own shell wrapper at TOOL_BIN = $TOOL_DIR/bin/dportsv3 and
an in-env venv at TOOL_VENV_RELATIVE = work/polytropos/.venv.

So the mount shadows a full, working checkout.

CONSEQUENCES OBSERVED ON x6

env_health_status went to broken:

    dports_compose: $POLYTROPOS_ROOT/bin/dportsv3 --version failed
    (rc=127): /bin/sh: /work/polytropos/bin/dportsv3: not found

rc=127 on a file that exists is the shebang: with the mount in place that
path resolves to a venv console script naming /usr/local/lib/polytropos/
bin/python, a HOST path absent from the chroot. worker.py's validate_dops
runs the identical command for `dsl check`, so patching is broken the
same way — health is just where it surfaced.

Unmounting proves it. With the mount gone, /work/polytropos/bin holds
agent-queue-runner, artifact-store, artifact-store-client and dportsv3,
and `/work/polytropos/bin/dportsv3 --version` prints 3.0.0-dev from
inside the chroot.

WHAT THIS SAYS ABOUT poly-7z1

Its premise was wrong. "In-chroot hooks cannot reach the tool" — they
could; the checkout has been there since env creation. The real defect
was narrower and is already fixed: dportsv3-hooks.conf shipped
DPORTSV3_BIN=/build/synth/polytropos/bin/dportsv3, a path on no machine,
when the answer was the checkout already mounted at TOOL_BIN. The bead
read the stale conf value as evidence the tool was absent.
design:
Revert the mount, and the machinery built to work around the shebang it created.

REMOVE
- runtime.TOOL_VENV_TARGET, tool_venv_target() and the mount in prepare_root_runtime
- config.tool_venv / DPORTS_DEV_TOOL_VENV
- POLYTROPOS_PYTHON and polytropos_run in hook_common.sh, and the -r/-x
  branch it added to tracker_load_config. The checkout wrapper is a shell
  script; no interpreter indirection is needed for anything.
- POLYTROPOS_PYTHON from env_hook_settings and the conf example

KEEP
- env_hook_settings writing DPORTSV3_BIN and ARTIFACT_STORE_CLIENT, but
  sourced from layout.TOOL_BIN / TOOL_DIR rather than the mount path.
  This is what poly-7z1 actually needed.
- DPORTSV3_TRACKER_TARGET from the env's target (poly-5v6), verified.
- the tracker_config_defaults split, which is independently correct: a
  hook with artifact-store work to do must not exit 0 because the tracker
  is unusable.
- artifact-store-client as a package module and console script; that
  fixed a real gap for packaged installs.

RESTORE
- bin/artifact-store-client in the checkout, as a stdlib-only shim that
  imports dportsv3.artifact_store_client. Moving it into the package fixed
  the packaged install and broke the checkout case, where the env's
  /work/polytropos/bin/artifact-store-client is what the hooks call. One
  implementation, two entry points.
acceptance_criteria: 1. env health reports ok for dports_compose with no manual step. 2. $POLYTROPOS_ROOT/bin/dportsv3 and $POLYTROPOS_ROOT/bin/artifact-store-client both run directly inside the chroot. 3. No mount lands on TOOL_DIR. 4. An env synced to this commit still has bin/artifact-store-client.
notes:
Fix committed as 6e9c7c5; NOT yet verified on hardware. Verification needs the env recreated, since x6's current env has the bind-mount live and four modules hand-installed into the host venv. Close only after env health reports dports_compose ok with no manual step.
VERIFIED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-27 after a full teardown: DB wiped, env destroyed and recreated from the fixed commit 05139c8.

- nothing mounts on TOOL_DIR (mount | grep work/polytropos is empty)
- the env's checkout is at 05139c8 and carries bin/artifact-store-client
- both tools run DIRECTLY in-chroot, no interpreter indirection:
  /work/polytropos/bin/dportsv3 --version -> 3.0.0-dev
  /work/polytropos/bin/artifact-store-client ... health -> ok
- env-health: python_runtime ok, writable_overlay ok, dports_compose ok
  (detail 'dportsv3 3.0.0-dev' — the exact probe that returned rc=127)
- hooks-install wrote DPORTSV3_BIN=/work/polytropos/bin/dportsv3 and
  ARTIFACT_STORE_CLIENT=/work/polytropos/bin/artifact-store-client, with
  no POLYTROPOS_PYTHON

title: Upgrading the rc.d scripts orphans a running stack
description:
The pidfile fix renamed what each file holds: the supervisor moved from \${name}.sup.pid to \${name}.pid, and the child moved to \${name}.child.pid. An operator upgrading a running stack keeps the old files, so `service stop|status` reads \${name}.pid, finds the CHILD pid there, fails to match procname (/usr/sbin/daemon) and reports 'not running' while all three services are alive. Observed on a live install: three running services, all reported not running, uncontrollable by service(8).

Consequence: the operator sees 'not running' and starts a second stack. The runner is protected by its flock (exit 3) but artifact-store and tracker race for their ports and share the DB.

The old processes have to be killed by pid, from the .sup.pid files, and those files removed. Nothing in deploy install does that or warns about it.
acceptance_criteria: 1) deploy install detects pidfiles from the previous layout and either refuses with the exact commands to run, or handles the changeover. 2) A running pre-change stack can be upgraded without the operator having to find pids by hand. 3) Documented in the runbook's 'when a service will not run' table.

title: Base-branch resolution reads the symlink and silently defaults to master
description:
_resolve_bundle_base_branch (worker.py) determines the branch every job worktree cuts from. Three problems, all found while auditing poly-m7o:

  * It runs 'cd /work/DeltaPorts' — the agent-facing symlink — when this is plumbing and should address PORTS_MAIN_DIR. layout.py is explicit that agent-facing code uses the symlink and plumbing names ports-main. Same class as the two stale tool paths in poly-iyk.
  * It swallows any failure into '|| echo master'. A dangling or mid-repoint link yields empty stdout and the base silently becomes 'master'.
  * The result is cached per env for the process lifetime, so one bad early read pins the wrong base for every job that runner handles.

For an env whose default branch is not master this produces worktrees cut from the wrong base, silently.

VERIFIED: the function's body, its use as 'base' in create_job_worktree, and that base is passed to 'git worktree add -b <branch> <wt> <base>'.
NOT VERIFIED: whether any env in practice has a non-master default. If they are all master the impact is latent rather than active — worth checking before prioritising.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Base resolution reads PORTS_MAIN_DIR, not the symlink. 2. A failed resolution is an error, not a silent 'master'. 3. The cache cannot pin a value derived from a failed read.
notes:
VERIFIED ACTIVE ON x6 2026-08-23, not latent. The bead said the impact was unknown until someone checked whether a real env has a non-master default. Checked, and that was the wrong question:

  git -C /work/ports-main symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD
  -> fatal: ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD is not a symbolic ref

The symbolic-ref FAILS on a real env, so '|| echo master' fires on EVERY call. The base is never actually resolved from the repo — it is always the hardcoded default, and the per-env cache then pins that for the process lifetime. _resolve_bundle_base_branch('2026Q3-editors_vim') returns 'master'.

Benign on this env only because ports-main happens to be on master (rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD = master, confirmed). Any env whose checkout sits on another branch gets worktrees cut from the wrong base, silently, with no diagnostic anywhere.

So this is not 'a fallback that might fire'. The resolution does not work at all; the right answer is currently arriving by coincidence.

LIKELY ROOT CAUSE to confirm when fixing: dev-env clones the ports mirror with 'git clone --mirror', and a mirror clone does not necessarily set refs/remotes/origin/HEAD. Worth checking whether the fix belongs in the clone (set origin/HEAD) as well as in the resolver (stop swallowing the failure).
CODE RE-REVIEW 2026-08-23. Root cause found in the tree, and it is stronger than the bead's guess.

ROOT CAUSE, VERIFIED: RepoCache.clone_branch clones the env's ports checkout with
  git clone --single-branch --branch <branch> <mirror> <dest>
--single-branch does not create refs/remotes/origin/HEAD. So the resolver's stated premise — 'rare; clones from a mirror usually have it' — is false BY CONSTRUCTION for every env dev-env builds. Not rare, universal. The bead listed this as a likely cause to confirm; it is confirmed, in repos.py, not just inferred from the x6 symptom.

CHOSEN FIX: resolve from the branch actually checked out in PORTS_MAIN_DIR —
  git -C /work/ports-main rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
Correct because clone_branch checks out exactly state.repos.deltaports_branch. Safe because nothing detaches that HEAD: sync.py's reset_env_repo does 'reset --hard <sha>' on the current branch (moves the branch pointer, stays symbolic) and update.py fast-forwards. Both were checked, and both already address PORTS_MAIN_RELATIVE explicitly with comments about not going through the symlink — the dev-env side already learned this lesson; only the agent resolver missed it. Works on EXISTING envs, which a clone-side fix would not.

NO SILENT DEFAULT: failure, empty output, or a literal 'HEAD' (detached) all mean resolution failed. Returned as a failure result rather than raised, matching the module's result-dict style: create_job_worktree returns ok=False with a clear error, and under poly-m7o the job is then retired worktree_unavailable instead of being cut from a guessed base. The two changes compose — a job never silently builds on the wrong base.

CACHE KEPT but only for successful resolutions. Its rationale still holds (a subprocess per call, and an env's base does not change during its lifetime); the bug was caching a value derived from a failed read.

CONSIDERED AND REJECTED — reading state.repos.deltaports_branch from the env state. More declarative, but couples the agent worker to the dev-env state schema and would disagree with reality if anyone switched branches in the env. 'What is actually checked out' is the better authority.

CONSIDERED AND DEFERRED — also setting origin/HEAD at clone time (git remote set-head). It would repair mirror semantics, but only for NEW envs, and nothing else in the tree consumes origin/HEAD for the ports tree (grepped: only this function). Worth doing if another consumer ever appears.

TESTS TO UPDATE: three files pin the current behaviour — test_changes_diff_semantics.py, test_dev_env_job_worktree.py, test_bundle_branch_lifecycle.py.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-23.

_resolve_bundle_base_branch now reads 'git -C /work/ports-main rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD' and returns str | None. A failed command, empty output, or a literal 'HEAD' (detached) all return None. create_job_worktree refuses with ok=False and a plain error rather than guessing, which under poly-m7o retires the job worktree_unavailable — so a job can never silently build on the wrong base. Only successful reads are cached.

TEST THAT PINNED THE BUG: test_base_branch_fallback_to_master asserted the '|| echo master' behaviour as intended, with a docstring explaining it. Replaced. Worth noting the bug had a passing test defending it.

A GAP IN MY OWN TEST, found by mutation: 'failures are not cached' initially passed even with the guard moved after the cache write, because a failed command yields base='' and the cache lookup is truthiness-based, so an empty value never sticks. The case that actually matters is detached HEAD — 'HEAD' is truthy, so it WOULD survive in the cache and be returned as a branch name forever after. The test is now parametrized over all three failure shapes and asserts the cache stays empty.

TOOLING HAZARD worth remembering: the first mutation run reported a false pass and then a false failure on restore. Cause was stale .pyc — the script rewrote worker.py fast enough that CPython's mtime+size invalidation did not trip. Mutation runs now clear __pycache__ between steps. Any earlier mutation result in this repo taken without clearing bytecode is suspect.

Five mutations, all caught after the fix: restoring the silent master fallback, reading the symlink instead of ports-main, accepting a detached HEAD, caching failures, and letting worktree creation proceed without a base. 2150 tests pass.

NOT YET VERIFIED ON x6 — needs the commit pushed so the test clone can pull. Expect: resolution returns 'master' for the right reason (rev-parse, not a fallback), and pointing ports-main at a detached HEAD makes create_job_worktree refuse.
VERIFIED ON x6 2026-08-23 against the live 2026Q3-editors_vim env.

A. ROOT CAUSE VISIBLE IN THE ENV'S OWN GIT CONFIG:
     remote.origin.fetch = +refs/heads/master:refs/remotes/origin/master
   A single-branch refspec — exactly what 'git clone --single-branch' writes, and why refs/remotes/origin/HEAD is absent ('fatal: ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD is not a symbolic ref', still). So the old resolver's read fails on this env today, and '|| echo master' was supplying every answer. This is the root cause confirmed from the env side, independently of reading repos.py.

B. The resolver now returns 'master' via rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD — the right answer for the right reason rather than by coincidence.

C. Refusal path exercised for real: detached ports-main HEAD -> _resolve_bundle_base_branch returned None and create_job_worktree returned ok=False with 'could not determine the base branch from /work/ports-main ... (detached HEAD, or the checkout is unreadable)'. No guess, no worktree. ports-main restored to master afterwards; env left clean.

All three acceptance criteria met.

title: Worktree-creation soft-fail can run a job against another job's tree
description:
_checkout_bundle_branch_for_job (runner.py:2720) is soft-fail by design: if create_job_worktree fails the job PROCEEDS. That rationale predates B1 and its docstring still describes the pre-B1 world — 'falls back to pre-Step-30 behavior (commits land on whatever branch is current)'. That was safe when the fallback was one shared checkout sitting on some branch.

After B1 the fallback is different in kind. create_job_worktree returns BEFORE _point_ports_link when 'worktree add' fails (worker.py:1588-1594), so /work/DeltaPorts keeps whatever it pointed at. Normally that is ports-main, because destroy_job_worktree repoints on job end. But if a previous job crashed or its teardown failed, the link still points at THAT job's worktree — so this job's agent edits a dead job's tree and its commits land on the dead job's branch. Cross-job contamination, which is the exact thing B1 exists to prevent.

NOT HYPOTHETICAL: create_job_worktree returned ok=False twice during B1 bring-up, both on the first call after deploying new code, never reproduced across 12 fresh cycles and never explained. The soft-fail path has fired for real.

CANDIDATE FIXES, not chosen: (a) hard-fail the job when the worktree cannot be created — the trade-off the original rationale rejected, but the cost of proceeding is now much higher than 'lost isolation'; (b) force the link to the idle target (ports-main) before proceeding, so a soft-fail degrades to the main checkout rather than to an arbitrary dead job's tree; (c) assert the link resolves to this job's worktree before any worker.* call.

(b) is the smallest change that removes the contamination while keeping the original soft-fail intent.

Also update the stale docstring rationale in runner.py:2731-2739 whichever way this lands.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A failed worktree creation cannot leave a job editing another job's tree. 2. The soft-fail rationale in _checkout_bundle_branch_for_job describes post-B1 behaviour. 3. The verify/confirm path (_checkout_verify_branch_for_job) gets the same treatment or a documented reason it differs.
notes:
CORRECTION 2026-08-23 — the recommendation above is WRONG. Do not implement option (b).

Option (b) was 'force the link to the idle target (ports-main) before proceeding, so a soft-fail degrades to the main checkout'. I wrote that without reading what the worktree cuts from. Having now read it:

  * create_job_worktree takes base from _resolve_bundle_base_branch, which returns a LOCAL BRANCH NAME (master by default), and cuts new bundle branches from it.
  * commit_port_changes runs 'cd /work/DeltaPorts && git add -A && git commit', i.e. into whatever the symlink points at, on whatever branch that tree has checked out.

So pointing the link at ports-main means the agent's commits land on the base branch itself — the branch every future worktree cuts from. That converts a single job's contamination into permanent poisoning of the base for all subsequent jobs. Strictly worse than the bug being fixed.

THERE IS NO SAFE FALLBACK TREE. That is the finding. Option (a), hard-fail, is the fix: no worktree, no job. A DEAD job is re-enqueueable; silent contamination is not detectable. The original soft-fail rationale ('failing hard would regress bundles that would otherwise run fine') assumed a benign fallback that B1 removed.

CRITERION 3 IS ALREADY SATISFIED, also unchecked when I wrote it: _checkout_verify_branch_for_job is explicitly NOT soft-fail and its docstring already gives the reason it differs — a failed checkout makes any verify verdict meaningless. Only the patch/convert path needs the change.

SEPARATE BUG FOUND WHILE CHECKING THIS, filed as its own bead: _resolve_bundle_base_branch resolves the base by cd-ing into /work/DeltaPorts (the agent-facing symlink) instead of PORTS_MAIN_DIR, swallows failure into '|| echo master', and caches per env.
IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-23 as hard-fail.

_checkout_bundle_branch_for_job now returns bool. process_patch_job retires the job (and its siblings) on False via a new lifecycle event, WORKTREE_UNAVAILABLE -> DEAD, retire_reason 'worktree_unavailable', and returns (False, 'worktree_unavailable') so the file lands in failed/ with an error note.

WHY A NEW EVENT RATHER THAN REUSING ONE — checked the consumers rather than assuming:
  * ENV_BROKEN feeds the health contract and decision.py's 'defer until healthy'. A git failure is not a broken env.
  * PATCH_GAVE_UP sets retire_reason 'patch_gave_up', which decision.py counts as a failed patch attempt to decide escalation. Machinery failures counted there would suppress future work on the port.
Two tests assert the new reason stays out of both signals.

STATE IT FIRES FROM: PATCHING. PATCH_START fires before the checkout in process_job, verified rather than assumed (patch_gave_up's only from-state is 'patching'). Transitions also added from CLAIMED and TRIAGED so a future earlier caller retires cleanly instead of hitting an IllegalTransition, which _apply_transition swallows.

A BUG THE TESTS CAUGHT: the call site referenced JobEvent, which is not bound at module scope in runner.py — every use is a local import. The module still imported fine because the reference sits inside a function body; only executing the path raises NameError. The call-site test executes it, and mutation-testing confirmed removing the import fails that test.

EXISTING TESTS I HAD TO CHANGE, disclosed: six tests in test_runner_orchestrator_parity.py broke, because create_job_worktree raises in the test env (no $DPORTSV3_CMD) and soft-fail used to absorb it. I stubbed create_job_worktree/destroy_job_worktree in that fixture, alongside the existing assert_port_clean stub and for the same stated reason — those tests exercise the orchestrator event chain, not worktree provisioning. Worth being clear this weakened them slightly rather than pretending they passed untouched.

ACCEPTED TRADE-OFF, NOT SOLVED: worktree_unavailable is terminal. A transient git failure now kills a job that would previously have run, and recovery is an operator re-enqueue from the bundle. That is the deliberate choice — a dead job is visible and recoverable, silent cross-job contamination is neither — but whether this class of failure should instead be retryable is a real question I did not answer. The queue has no retry mechanism I verified.

NOT VERIFIED IN A REAL CHROOT (poly-4kr). Everything above is unit-level plus mutation testing.
PARTIALLY VERIFIED ON x6 2026-08-23. The helper's contract holds against a real chroot: _checkout_bundle_branch_for_job returned False for an env that cannot produce a worktree (logged 'worktree add for bundle/b1 failed'), and True as a no-op when bundle_id is absent.

NOT verified: the call site retiring a real patch job worktree_unavailable, which still needs a live LLM job (poly-4kr).

title: Two in-chroot call sites still located the tool in the ports tree (runner could not start)
description:
Missed by the X5/X6 repository split. Both invoked the wrapper as "$DELTAPORTS_ROOT/dportsv3", which is two mistakes at once: DELTAPORTS_ROOT is the ports tree, not the tool checkout, and in this repo the repo-root 'dportsv3' name belongs to the Python package rather than the wrapper (the wrapper is bin/dportsv3). layout.py:50 documents that exact trap; these two consumers were not repointed.

  * health.py:236 _check_dports_compose — SEVERITY: total. sh returns 127, the check reports broken, _aggregate turns any broken check into a broken env, and _gate_blocked pauses the whole runner loop. The runner could not process a single job in any env built after the split.
  * worker.py:1746 validate_dops — the convert agent's cheap dsl check always failed.

Confirmed /work/DeltaPorts/dportsv3 does not exist post-split by inspecting a real DeltaPorts checkout: the repo has no dportsv3 at its root, so there was no stale vendored copy masking this.

CORROBORATING SIGNAL, worth remembering as a smell: build_env_dict has exported POLYTROPOS_ROOT since the split (helpers.py:148) and NOTHING consumed it except the showenv helper and tests. A new env var with no readers meant the consumers were never repointed.

WHY THE X5 VERIFICATION MISSED IT: criterion 5 was verified on x6 by provisioning an env, not by running the runner loop. Provisioning uses TOOL_BIN and is correct; the health gate and the agent tool path are only exercised once the runner actually starts, which poly-4kr blocks.

FIXED: both call sites now use "$POLYTROPOS_ROOT/bin/dportsv3". tests/test_chroot_tool_path.py greps the whole agent package for the old shape and asserts the built command text for both helpers; mutation-tested by reverting each fix.

STILL OPEN, low priority: docs/agentic-architecture-backlog.md:1214 shows the old invocation. Historical design record, but a copy-paste re-infection source.

NOT VERIFIED IN A REAL CHROOT — no way to run the services yet (poly-4kr). The fix is a path correction with a unit guard; an end-to-end confirmation still owes.
acceptance_criteria: 1. No agent-package call site locates the wrapper under the ports tree. 2. A post-split env passes the compose health check so the runner does not pause. 3. Verified in a real chroot once poly-4kr unblocks.
notes:
AUDIT 2026-08-23. Everything in this bead was verified by reading the code, checking a real DeltaPorts checkout for the absent wrapper, and mutation-testing the guard — with one exception already stated: the fix has NOT been confirmed in a real chroot, because poly-4kr blocks running the services.

Line numbers are stale post-fix: the call sites are _check_dports_compose in health.py and validate_dops in worker.py.
VERIFIED ON x6 2026-08-23 — acceptance criterion 3 met, the fix is confirmed on real hardware.

In the live env 2026Q3-editors_vim:
  DELTAPORTS_ROOT=/work/DeltaPorts   POLYTROPOS_ROOT=/work/polytropos
  old path $DELTAPORTS_ROOT/dportsv3      -> MISSING
  new path $POLYTROPOS_ROOT/bin/dportsv3  -> EXISTS

health.check() now returns STATUS: ready with dports_compose ok ('dportsv3 3.0.0-dev'). Before the fix that check returned broken, _aggregate turned the env broken and _gate_blocked paused the runner outright, so this confirms both the bug and the fix on hardware.

title: reconcile/diff_tree silently miss content changes: _DeepDircmp.phase3 override never runs
description: fsutils._DeepDircmp overrides phase3 to force cmpfiles(shallow=False) so classification is content-based. The override is NEVER CALLED. filecmp.dircmp.methodmap is built in the class body and captures the BASE class function objects; dircmp.__getattr__ dispatches via self.methodmap[attr](self), which invokes dircmp.phase3, not the subclass override. Verified on Python 3.11.12 (DragonFly x6) and 3.11.14 (macOS): methodmap['same_files'] is <function dircmp.phase3>, and two files with equal size+mtime but different content classify as same_files. Consequence: reconcile() skips the copy and diff_tree() reports no difference, so a real content change is silently lost. Masked on macOS/APFS because nanosecond mtime makes consecutive writes differ (1787237401268667053 vs ...740553), so the accidental shallow compare still sees a diff. Exposed on DragonFly/HAMMER2 where consecutive writes share an mtime (both 1787237404520528000) - the production platform. Realistic trigger: a same-length edit such as DISTVERSION=1.2.3 -> 1.2.4 written in one tick would not propagate to the live composed tree. Surfaced as 3 suite failures on x6: test_fsutils_reconcile.py::test_content_change_updates_dst, ::test_symlinks_with_different_content_replaced, test_fsutils_diff_tree.py::test_content_difference_is_reported.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Content-based classification actually runs - do not rely on overriding phase3. 2) A regression test pins the failure mode directly: equal size AND equal mtime, different content, must classify as a difference on every platform (force mtimes equal with os.utime so it fails on macOS too, rather than depending on filesystem granularity). 3) The three x6 failures pass. 4) Audit other dircmp/filecmp subclassing for the same methodmap trap.
notes: Hash correction: the fix commit is 4af664d (referenced as 06546ff before the attribution trailer was stripped and the unpushed commits rewritten).
close_reason: Fixed in 06546ff. _DeepDircmp.phase3 was never invoked (dircmp.methodmap binds base-class functions); the three attributes are now filled eagerly in __init__ so they shadow the lazy dispatch. Regression tests force equal size+mtime via os.utime so they fail on macOS too, not only on HAMMER2. Mutation-tested: both new tests fail with the fix disabled. Also corrected test_content_change_updates_dst, whose mtime assertion was itself granularity-dependent. 2089 passed on macOS 3.11.14 and DragonFly 3.11.12.

title: X5 Chroot: provision from two repos, keep /work/DeltaPorts unchanged
description:
The deepest coupling. Re-verified 2026-08-20 against the post-split tree; the
original notes were written pre-X8 and are corrected here.

WHAT BREAKS FIRST (not previously recorded): builder.py:154 validates the ports
tree by requiring a `dportsv3` file inside --delta-root ("Delta root does not
look like this repo") — a fossil from when the tool and the ports tree were one
checkout. X8 deleted DeltaPorts/dportsv3, so `dev-env create` now fails at
validation, before mirrors, chroot or venv. The venv failure described below is
unreachable until this is fixed.

THEN: dev-env clones exactly one repo to work/DeltaPorts (update.py:33-36
ENV_REPOS, builder.py:111), installs the generator venv from inside that
checkout (venv.py:24 requires work/DeltaPorts/scripts/generator/pyproject.toml,
venv.py:33 installs to .../.venv) and probes readiness with
/work/DeltaPorts/dportsv3 compose --help (venv.py:50, 72).

CORRECTION: hooks.py:50 is already fixed. X1 replaced the parents-walk with
package-local data in repo_hook_source(). Nothing to do there.

ALSO MISSING FROM THE ORIGINAL LIST:
- repos.py:13-27 RepoMirrors is a frozen 3-field dataclass with no slot for the
  tool repo; refresh_all() mirrors exactly 3 repos.
- state.py:24-25 SourceState has only delta_root — nowhere to record which tool
  checkout an env was built from.
- sync.py:15,91 GENERATOR_VENV_RELATIVE = scripts/generator/.venv, a dead path
  used to exclude the venv from git clean.
- builder.py:158-163 the dirty check and --allow-dirty cover only the ports
  checkout; post-split it is TOOL dirtiness that decides what reaches the chroot.

CRITICAL CONSTRAINT (unchanged): /work/DeltaPorts must keep meaning 'the ports
tree'. It is the agent's only legal edit surface — hardcoded in LLM prompt text
(prompts.py:146-360, tools.py:118) and enforced by guardrails that reject other
prefixes (worker.py:213, 251-258). The ports tree stays; the TOOL gets a second
path. cli.py:327,413,440,475 operate on the ports overlay and are correct as-is.

DESIGN AGREED:

title: Worklist has no landing place for issues knocked off the happy path
description:
The issue worklist (/agentic, build_issue_worklist) silently loses or mislabels issues that leave the accept->deliver happy path. Two verified cases, one root cause: issue_bucket derives the band from the ACTIONABLE OCCURRENCE's resolution, so anything that changes the issue without changing its bundle (or blanks the bundle) lands wrong.

CASE 1 — red confirm build still reads 'Awaiting delivery'. reopen_issue_build_failed sets state='unresolved' and nulls delivery_bundle_id but does NOT touch the bundle, whose resolution stays 'accepted'. issue_bucket falls through and returns 'delivering' for occ_key=='accepted'. So a red confirm moves the issue from one looks-fixed band (resolving) to another (awaiting delivery) instead of 'decide'. A3's stated goal — stop an unfixed issue looking as good as fixed — is defeated. The only real signal is manual_handoff.md on a bundle the operator has no reason to open.

CASE 2 — operator bundle-reopen makes the issue VANISH. Reopening a bundle sets bundles.resolution to NULL -> fix_state.fix_status = 'unknown' -> worklist_bucket = None -> issue_bucket returns None -> build_issue_worklist DROPS it (issue_state.py:257-258, 'Issues that aren't operator-actionable right now (bucket None) are omitted'). The issue disappears from /agentic entirely and is only findable on /agentic/issues. Bucket None means 'the runner is working it, nothing to do yet', which is exactly wrong for an issue an operator just reopened by hand.

Reproduced live on the demo DB: iss-queued and iss-redconfirm both sat at bucket=None and were absent from the dashboard worklist while still listed on /agentic/issues. Confirmed via the events audit log that the state writes themselves were all correct — this is purely a projection/UX hole, not state corruption.

Compounding UX factor: there are two different Reopen buttons (bundle-level and issue-level) whose effects differ (bundle reopen never changes issue state), with nothing in the UI explaining which one moves what.
acceptance_criteria: 1) An issue whose confirm build went red lands in an actionable band (decide), not delivering. 2) An issue whose bundle an operator reopened stays VISIBLE in the worklist in an actionable band, instead of being dropped by the bucket-None rule. 3) Decide whether the bundle's resolution should move off 'accepted' when its confirm build fails. 4) Bucket None is reserved for genuinely runner-owned work; operator-touched issues never fall into it. 5) The red verdict + handoff are reachable from the issue, not only from the bundle artifact. 6) The two Reopen actions are distinguishable in the UI (what each one moves). 7) Tests pin the bucket for (a) reopened-by-red-confirm and (b) operator-reopened bundle.
close_reason: Fixed: unknown -> decide (bucket None now reserved for runner-owned work), and accepted-occurrence-on-open-issue -> decide (stale pre-resolving branch). Plus 'confirming' added to _INFLIGHT_JOB_STATES. Demo worklist 4/8 -> 8/8.

title: Confirm loop: duplicate builds on restart / lock contention / multi-runner
description: Adversarial review found 3 verified double-enqueue paths, each costing a full dsynth build. (a) RESTART: _reset_building_markers clears every building_generation at startup, but a confirm job sitting in pending/ SURVIVES — reap_orphans deliberately leaves QUEUED claimable (lifecycle.py:476 'QUEUED stays queued') and reap_stale_queued only reaps rows whose .job file is missing. So the old job is still claimable AND the feed enqueues a fresh one: two builds, two greens, and with the A4 threshold of 2 the issue resolves on what was effectively one requested confirmation. (b) NON-ATOMIC MARK: process_build_requests enqueues the job file and only then calls _mark_issue_building, which swallows sqlite3.Error and returns silently when the conn is None. If the tracker holds the write lock past busy_timeout the marker is never set, nothing is logged, and the next loop pass (<=5s) enqueues a duplicate. (c) MULTI-RUNNER: a second runner's startup sweep wipes the first runner's live in-flight markers.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A queued-but-unclaimed confirm job is reconciled on restart rather than duplicated (reap it, or make the marker sweep aware of pending confirm jobs). 2) Enqueue+mark is atomic, or the mark failing prevents/undoes the enqueue and is logged. 3) Multi-runner startup does not clear another live runner's markers. 4) Tests cover all three.
close_reason: Fixed the two in-scope paths: claim-before-enqueue (CAS, failed claim never enqueues) and coherent restart sweep (discard queued confirm jobs + clear markers, then re-derive). Multi-runner filed separately as a pre-existing system-wide gap.

title: Confirm loop: issue stuck in resolving on permanently-doomed builds
description: A machinery gave-up deliberately leaves building_generation set to avoid hot-looping a broken env, and ONLY the startup _reset_building_markers clears it. Consequences verified: (a) a long-lived runner parks the issue in resolving forever with no retry, no backoff and no operator-visible signal beyond one activity row; recovery requires a human restarting the runner, which is documented nowhere operator-facing. (b) PERMANENTLY-DOOMED builds loop: run_verify_fix raises VerifyFixError when the bundle has no changes.diff or it is empty (verify_fix.py:206-215), and the dispatch raises when no dev-env is available — so every restart clears the marker, re-enqueues, raises again, re-sets the marker. The issue never leaves resolving and each restart burns a job. Operator escape hatch does exist (manual resolve/reopen are allowed from resolving, issue_state.py:59-60) but is undiscoverable. Overlaps C4 (per-key backoff).
acceptance_criteria: 1) A doomed confirm (missing/empty changes.diff, no dev-env) is detected and does not retry indefinitely — terminal state + operator signal. 2) A stalled in-flight marker is recoverable without a runner restart. 3) The operator can see WHY an issue is parked in resolving. 4) Coordinate with C4 backoff so the two do not conflict.
close_reason: Fixed: machinery failures now clear the marker and retry without a restart, bounded by DP_CONFIRM_MAX_FAILURES (default 3), after which the issue is reopened with a manual handoff. Pacing (per-key backoff) remains C4.

title: A2 Green -> resolved (build-confirmed) + Green Head
description: A2 Green -> resolved (build-confirmed). On a green confirm build, advance the issue resolving->resolved and record the Green-Head build ordinal per (target,origin). Read-only on build_* (reads port_status).
design:
## Design

On a GREEN confirm-build verdict (from A1's report-back), make the build — not the
merge — the authority that resolves the issue.

**Transition:** in the confirm-build report-back handler, when verdict=green for the
issue currently in `resolving`:
- `state: resolving -> resolved`, `resolved_at = now`, source `'build-confirmed'`
  (reuse the `resolve_issue` writer, issue_actions.py:83, or an inline UPDATE with
  the same shape/event).
- GUARD: only from `state='resolving'` (mirror `mark_issue_resolving`'s
  `WHERE state IN (...)`, issue_actions.py:112) so a muted / unresolved / already-
  resolved issue is untouched.
- advance `last_confirmed_build_generation = generation`, clear `building_generation`.

**Green Head:** record the build ordinal at which (target, origin) went green — from
`port_status.last_success_run_id` / `build_runs.id` (schema.py:384/355). Store it as
`green_head_run_id` on the issue (new column) or a small `issue_green_head` side
row. This is the "known-good boundary" C3 derives `regressed` against (a later build
re-emitting the fingerprint at an ordinal > green head = regression).

**Authority shift (the point of the feature):** today `delivery_sync.py:148`
(`set_bundle_merged_resolution`) flips `resolved` on PR merge. A2 moves that
authority to the green build. For the MVP, merge becomes an OBSERVATION that no
longer directly resolves; the clean two-axis split (resolution vs build-observation)
is C3. Keep the change minimal here — do not delete the merge path yet, just stop
treating merge as the resolve trigger for issues that went through `resolving`.

**Emits** `issue_resolved` with `source='build-confirmed'` + `green_head_run_id`.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Green verdict for a resolving issue -> state resolving->resolved, resolved_at set, source=build-confirmed, event emitted. 2) Guard: transition only from state=resolving (muted/unresolved/resolved untouched). 3) Green-Head ordinal per (target,origin) recorded (green_head_run_id from port_status.last_success_run_id/build_runs.id). 4) last_confirmed_build_generation advanced, building_generation cleared (no re-enqueue). 5) Merge no longer directly flips resolved for issues that went through resolving (authority moves to the build; full split is C3; merge path not deleted yet). 6) Test: resolving+green -> resolved w/ green-head; muted+green -> untouched.
close_reason: Implemented + reviewed + committed. Green head implemented as a build_runs watermark (not port_status.last_success_run_id) because dsynth hooks are disabled in the dev-env so confirm builds never reach build_runs/port_status.

title: C1 Build intent (generation counter / build_requests)
description: C1 Build intent. The resolving transition writes desired build state — a generation counter on the issue (requested_build_generation) or a build_requests row. Crash-safe, self-dedup. Prior art: K8s observedGeneration.
design:
## Design

Record *desired build state* on the issue row when a fix is accepted, as a
monotonic generation counter — the level-triggered spine (K8s observedGeneration),
NOT an edge-triggered command.

**Schema (db/schema.py, `issues` table):**
- add `requested_build_generation INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`
- add `last_confirmed_build_generation INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`
- add `building_generation INTEGER` (NULL = no build in flight; single-flight marker, set by C2)

**Write point — `mark_issue_resolving` (tracker/routes/issue_actions.py:98):**
Extend the existing single UPDATE (the one that sets `state='resolving'`,
`delivery_bundle_id`) to also bump `requested_build_generation =
requested_build_generation + 1`, in the SAME statement / same txn. This is the
"record intent" half of the verify_requests pattern (agentic_api.py:533), but on
the issue row itself rather than an append table — so it is level-triggered and
self-dedups (a re-accept just bumps the counter; no duplicate queue rows — that is
C2's job).

**Read feed for C2:** a query helper (tracker/agentic_queries/issues.py) returning
issues where `state='resolving' AND requested_build_generation >
last_confirmed_build_generation AND (building_generation IS NULL OR
building_generation < requested_build_generation)`.

**Event:** extend the emitted `issue_resolving` event (issue_actions.py:117) to
carry `requested_build_generation`, or emit a companion `issue_build_requested`.

**Rejected alternative:** a `build_requests` append table mirroring verify_requests
exactly. Rejected because it is edge-triggered — it can drift (a request row says
done while state later regresses) and needs its own dedup. The counter-on-issue is
crash-safe by construction (one row, one UPDATE) and is what C2/A2 compare against.

**Why crash-safe:** the generation bump rides the same single UPDATE as the state
write, under the caller's BEGIN IMMEDIATE txn — a crash leaves either the old or the
new generation, never a half-written intent.
acceptance_criteria: 1) issues table gains requested_build_generation, last_confirmed_build_generation, building_generation. 2) mark_issue_resolving bumps requested_build_generation +1 in the same UPDATE that sets state=resolving (one statement, same txn). 3) Emits an event carrying the new generation. 4) A read helper returns issues where state=resolving AND requested>confirmed AND not in-flight. 5) Test: accept -> gen=1/state=resolving; re-accept newer bundle -> gen=2; crash between leaves old-or-new gen, never half.
close_reason: Implemented + unit-verified; committed 7eaa21a2624 (C1/C2) and d75906b8877 (A1 + C2 go-live). Real build path needs a live chroot to exercise.

title: Block C — Reconcile seam: level-triggered build trigger
description: Wire the build-trigger as level-triggered intent, not a command. The resolving transition writes desired state; the runner re-derives 'does a build need to exist?' each loop and stays sole queue writer. Same shape as verify_requests; tracker never touches the queue filesystem. Prior art: Kubernetes controllers, ArgoCD, Sentry.
close_reason: All four children delivered. The confirm-build trigger is level-triggered intent: the tracker bumps a generation counter, the runner re-derives what needs building each pass and stays sole queue writer, regressed is derived from the build record rather than stored, and the retries are counted and paced.

title: A1 Confirm-build execution
description: A1 Confirm-build execution — build (target,origin) with the accepted fix and report green/red, via a runner-dispatched job reusing dev-env apply-and-build / dsynth build. Cleaner once the build runs on Block B isolated worktree substrate (sequencing is a preference, not a hard dep).
design:
## Design

Execute the confirm-build and report a green/red verdict, REUSING the existing
in-process build-and-report machinery — no new build engine.

**Enqueue + dispatch:**
- `enqueue_confirm_build_job(queue_root, *, issue_key, bundle_id, origin, target,
  generation, env, requested_by)` — mirror `enqueue_verify_job` (runner.py:1850);
  new job `type=confirm`, carries `issue_key` + `generation` so the verdict can be
  tied back to the exact C1 intent.
- Runner dispatch arm handles `type=confirm` by calling
  `dportsv3.verify_fix.run_verify_fix` in-process (same path the verify job uses) —
  it applies the accepted fix (the `delivery_bundle_id` diff) and drives dev-env
  `apply-and-build` → dsynth build for (target, origin).

**Verdict source (dsynth-owned, read-only):** the build reports through the
existing hook path into `build_results` / `port_status` (schema.py:367/378) — we do
NOT write those core columns ourselves (the "dsynth owns build data" constraint).
Read `port_status.last_attempt_result` / `last_success_run_id` for the verdict, or
capture run_verify_fix's returned status.

**Report-back:** POST the verdict to a new tracker endpoint (mirror verify's
`POST /api/bundles/{id}/verification`), carrying `(issue_key, generation, verdict,
build_run_id)`. That endpoint hands off to A2 (green) / A3 (red).

**Generation bookkeeping:** whatever the outcome, set
`last_confirmed_build_generation = generation` and clear `building_generation` — so
the C2 loop stops re-enqueuing this generation. (A2 additionally resolves on green;
A3 reopens on red.)

**Block B note:** runs correctly on today's shared checkout; cleaner/safer on the
Block B per-job worktree substrate, but that is a preference, not a hard dependency.
acceptance_criteria: 1) enqueue_confirm_build_job + a type=confirm dispatch handler that runs the accepted fix through verify_fix.run_verify_fix (reused, no new build engine) for (target,origin). 2) Produces a structured green/red verdict tied to (issue_key, generation, target, origin, build_run_id). 3) Reads port_status read-only; does NOT write dsynth-owned build_* core columns. 4) Verdict POSTs back to a new tracker endpoint that routes to A2/A3. 5) Regardless of outcome, sets last_confirmed_build_generation=generation and clears building_generation. 6) Test: stubbed green -> verdict green vs generation; stubbed red -> verdict red.
close_reason: Implemented + unit-verified; committed 7eaa21a2624 (C1/C2) and d75906b8877 (A1 + C2 go-live). Real build path needs a live chroot to exercise.

title: C2 Runner reconcile loop (level-triggered)
description: C2 Runner reconcile loop (level-triggered). Each loop, re-derive needs-a-build (requested_gen > last_built_gen) and enqueue a confirm-build job; runner is sole queue writer. Mirrors process_verify_requests. Prior art: K8s level-triggered reconcile + resync.
design:
## Design

New `process_build_requests(queue_root)` in agent/runner.py, a near-clone of
`process_verify_requests` (runner.py:880), called from the main loop right next to
it (runner.py:3831). Level-triggered: each pass RE-DERIVES which issues need a build
rather than draining a command queue.

**Each pass:**
1. SELECT the C1 feed — issues with `state='resolving' AND
   requested_build_generation > last_confirmed_build_generation` and not already
   in flight (`building_generation IS NULL OR < requested_build_generation`).
2. For each, look up `delivery_bundle_id` → its origin/target (mirror the bundle
   lookup at runner.py:919).
3. Call a new `enqueue_confirm_build_job(...)` (mirror `enqueue_verify_job`,
   runner.py:1850; new job `type=confirm`).
4. Single-flight mark: set `building_generation = requested_build_generation` for
   that issue (mirror `_mark_verify_request`, runner.py:953) so the next loop pass
   does NOT re-enqueue while the build runs. A1/A2 clear/advance it on completion.

**Invariants preserved:**
- Runner is the SOLE writer to the queue filesystem; the tracker only wrote the
  intent counter (C1). Restores the tracker-is-read-only-for-queue rule, same as
  verify_requests.
- Env selection reuses `env_resolver` (per-job dev-env precedence).

**'env busy' vs real failure (MVP):** if no env is free, skip and retry next loop
(no penalty, no in-flight mark). Per-key exponential backoff for *real* failures is
C4 — not needed for the MVP.

**Resync:** because it re-derives from the counter every pass, a lost enqueue or a
runner restart self-heals — the issue still shows requested > confirmed next loop.
acceptance_criteria: 1) process_build_requests(queue_root) added, called from the runner main loop next to process_verify_requests. 2) Each pass re-derives issues needing a build (requested>confirmed, state=resolving, not in-flight) and enqueues one confirm-build job per (target,origin,delivery_bundle_id) via enqueue_confirm_build_job. 3) Runner is the sole queue-fs writer; tracker wrote only the counter. 4) Single-flight: two loop passes before the build finishes enqueue exactly ONE job (building_generation marker). 5) env-busy -> skip/retry next loop, no penalty, no in-flight mark. 6) Test: seeded resolving issue -> one job; second pass -> none.
notes: Mechanism implemented + smoke-verified (enqueue_confirm_build_job, process_build_requests, _mark_issue_building single-flight, _reset_building_markers crash-recovery). NOT wired into the runner main loop yet: the loop call + _reset_building_markers startup call land WITH A1 (DeltaPorts-rk0), because C1 already creates resolving issues and a type=confirm job has no dispatch handler until A1. Producer+consumer go live atomically. Confirm-specific lifecycle transitions (CONFIRM_START/GREEN/RED) are A1's.
close_reason: Implemented + unit-verified; committed 7eaa21a2624 (C1/C2) and d75906b8877 (A1 + C2 go-live). Real build path needs a live chroot to exercise.

title: Block A — Execution oracle: gate `resolved` on a build, not the merge
description: Stop trusting the PR-merge event; make `resolved` mean the port actually builds. Reuses verify_fix.py build-and-report machinery; reads dsynth-owned port_status read-only; joins on (target,origin,fingerprint). Prior art: ClusterFuzz progression, SWE-bench, Google TAP.

title: A packaged install has no 'dportsv3 dev-env', but the docs tell operators to use it
description:
docs/OPERATOR_SETUP.md instructs 'bin/dportsv3 dev-env hooks-install myenv' and 'bin/dportsv3 dev-env shell'. That works from a checkout, because the repo's bin/dportsv3 shell wrapper routes dev-env by exec'ing dports-dev-env (worker.py documents the same three-way resolution).

The installed /usr/local/bin/dportsv3 is a venv console script for dportsv3.cli:main, which has no such subcommand:

  dportsv3: error: argument COMMAND: invalid choice: 'dev-env'
  (choose from 'compose', 'compose-report', 'dsl', 'migrate', 'tracker',
   'artifact-store', 'agent-queue-runner', 'deploy', 'verify-fix',
   'env-health')

So on a deployed host every dev-env instruction in the operator docs fails, and the operator has to discover that the command is actually dports-dev-env. Confusingly the dev-env CLI still prints its usage as 'dportsv3 dev-env create', which reinforces the wrong invocation.
design:
Either route dev-env from dportsv3.cli the way the checkout wrapper does — exec the dports-dev-env entry point, which deploy already links into the prefix — or change the docs and the dev-env CLI's own prog name to say dports-dev-env consistently.

Routing is preferable: one command name for operators, and it matches what the docs, the wrapper and the CLI's usage string all already claim.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The invocation in OPERATOR_SETUP.md works on a packaged install. 2. The usage string and the working command agree.
notes: Same class, another instance: env_health_status.operator_action tells the operator to 'run `dportsv3 dev-env health <env>`'. There is no such command — dev-env has no health action, and the probe is `dportsv3 env-health <env>`. So the guidance printed when an env is broken names a command that does not exist, in a tool where the same string is stored in the DB and shown in the UI.

title: A stale active build_runs row silently disables tracking for every later build
description:
hook_run_start calls 'dportsv3 tracker start-build'. If a previous run left a build_runs row with finished_at NULL, the tracker returns 409 and the hook responds by setting TRACKING_DISABLED=1 for the whole run.

Observed on x6 2026-08-27: a run started 2026-08-26T23:22:35 never got its hook_run_end, so the row stayed active. Every subsequent in-env build gets:

  tracking disabled for profile=2026Q3-editors_vim: start-build failed:
  Tracker API error (409) for POST /api/builds: Active build already
  exists for @2026Q3 test: run 2

Consequence: no build_runs ordinal is minted, so occurrences arrive with build_run_id NULL and the C3 regression derivation silently falls back to wall-clock timestamps — the exact comparison C3 exists to avoid. Nothing surfaces in the UI; the only trace is a line in the hook log.

runner.py's dsynth_active already documents the same class of staleness: 'build_runs.finished_at can be stale (operator ^C'd dsynth, hook_run_end never ran, row left at NULL forever)' — and deliberately refuses to use it as a gate for that reason. start-build has no such defence.
design:
Options, cheapest first.

1. Let start-build adopt or supersede a stale active run past some age, rather than 409ing. An active run older than any plausible build is not active.
2. Have hook_run_start retry once after asking the tracker to close a stale run, so an interrupted build self-heals on the next attempt.
3. Surface it: an active run with no heartbeat should show as stale in the UI instead of being invisible until it blocks something.

Whatever the mechanism, the failure mode to remove is that tracking silently degrades to timestamps. If tracking cannot start, that should be visible where someone looks, not only in the hook log.
acceptance_criteria: 1. An interrupted build does not disable tracking for every subsequent build. 2. When tracking does get disabled, it is visible outside the hook log. 3. C3's ordinal comparison is not silently downgraded to wall clocks.

title: The log distiller has no patterns for ports/bmake failures
description:
distill_log's "First error candidates" section came back empty for all
three real DragonFly ports failures captured on x6 — a patch-phase
failure (devel/glib20@bootstrap), a fetch failure (lang/rust), and one
line for a configure failure (graphics/jpeg-turbo).

The pattern list is compiler and build-system vocabulary: fatal error:,
undefined reference, ld: error:, collect2: error, CMake Error,
configure: error, meson.build:.*ERROR, ninja: build stopped, error:
failed to run custom build command for, "ERROR: ", No such file or
directory.

None of the ports vocabulary is there:

    *** Error code N        the bmake marker on EVERY ports failure
    Stop.                   bmake, immediately after
    ===>  FAILED ...        the patch phase
    FAILED to apply cleanly the patch phase
    N out of M hunks failed patch(1) reject
    FAILED 00:00:01         dsynth's own phase marker

So for the two most ports-specific failure classes the section is
completely empty, and errors.txt carries the failure only inside its
"Tail (last 200 lines)" block.

WHY THAT IS NOT GOOD ENOUGH

It worked here by luck of shape: a patch failure, a fetch failure and a
configure failure all stop the build immediately, so the error IS the
tail. A compile failure does not — bmake keeps other jobs running and
prints their output after the first error. With Max_jobs_per_builder
raised (2 -> 4 on x6 today) that window widens, and the first error can
fall outside a 200-line tail. errors.txt is what triage reads first, so
the failure would simply not be in the evidence.

Verified against the bundle the store actually holds, not by reading the
script: devel_glib20@bootstrap-20260827-105701Z, logs/errors.txt, 188
lines, failure text at lines 178-182.
design:
Add the ports vocabulary to both grep -nE lists in distill_log (candidates and error blocks). At minimum: '\*\*\* Error code', 'FAILED to apply', 'hunks failed', '===>  FAILED'. Keep them anchored where possible so a port that merely prints the phrase does not flood the section.

Worth pairing with a test that runs distill_log over a captured real ports log and asserts the failure line appears in the CANDIDATES section, not just the tail — the tail masks this bug, so a test that only greps the whole file would pass today.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A patch-phase failure and a bmake 'Error code' failure both appear in First error candidates. 2. A failure occurring more than 200 lines before the end of the log still reaches errors.txt.
notes: RECONFIRMED 2026-08-27 on the clean stack, devel_glib20@bootstrap-20260827-120810Z: errors.txt is 188 lines, the 'First error candidates' section has ZERO non-blank lines, and the failure appears only at lines 178/181 inside the 200-line tail. Same for the other two failures of the run.

title: The deployed venv is not self-contained, so it half-works when bind-mounted
description:
deploy install builds the venv with --system-site-packages, deliberately:
DragonFly pkgs supply modules pip cannot build there (see poly-170). The
venv therefore imports part of its dependency set from
/usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages on the HOST.

That breaks the moment the venv is bind-mounted into a dev-env chroot.
The venv's own lib travels with the mount; what it inherited from the
host's system site-packages does not, and the chroot's
/usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages is a different, emptier
directory.

Observed on x6 after mounting the venv at /work/polytropos: python
resolves correctly (sys.prefix=/work/polytropos, 3.11.12, matching the
host) and artifact-store-client works, because it is stdlib-only.
dportsv3 dies at import with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named
'tomli_w'. Full gap was tomli_w, tomli, requests, packaging — all
pure-Python, all present on the host only via system site-packages.

Consequence: the artifact-store half of the hooks works in-chroot and the
tracker half does not, which reads as a tracker outage rather than a
packaging problem.

Worked around by hand on x6:

    pip install --ignore-installed tomli_w tomli requests packaging

into the venv. Note that plain "pip install" is a no-op here — with
--system-site-packages pip sees the host copies and reports them already
satisfied, exits 0, and installs nothing. That workaround is operator
improvisation and is lost on the next deploy install.
design:
Two candidate fixes.

1. Make the venv self-contained for anything pure-Python. deploy install already knows the distribution set; have it force pure-Python deps into the venv (--ignore-installed) so nothing it needs is inherited. Keeps --system-site-packages for the compiled modules that genuinely need to come from pkg, which are the reason it exists.

2. Install the same pkgs inside the env base. Loses on version skew and repeats per env.

(1) is preferred: one venv, self-contained, mountable anywhere. It also makes the relocation property explicit rather than accidental — the venv is a deployment artifact that gets bind-mounted, so depending on the host's site-packages is a bug by construction.

Worth a test that imports every top-level dependency with the system site-packages hidden (PYTHONNOUSERSITE + a stripped sys.path), so the gap is caught in CI rather than on a chroot.
acceptance_criteria: 1. dportsv3 runs inside a dev-env chroot straight after deploy install, with no manual pip step. 2. The check is automated, not a runbook note. 3. --system-site-packages still covers the compiled modules that need it.
notes: OBSOLETE — superseded by poly-svh. The premise was 'the venv breaks when bind-mounted into a chroot', and 6e9c7c5 removes the bind-mount. Envs reach the tool through the checkout at TOOL_DIR, which builds its own venv inside the chroot from the chroot's python, so nothing is inherited from the host's system site-packages. The four modules that had to be force-installed on x6 were only needed to prop up the mount.

title: In-env hook outputs are chroot paths the host cannot resolve
description:
Split out of poly-7z1's fourth part so that bead stays closable on its own scope (tool reachability, which is fixed and verified).

Reaching the tools was necessary but not sufficient. Two of hook_pkg_failure's outputs are PATHS, and inside a chroot they are chroot paths nothing on the host can resolve.

1. THE QUEUE. queue_root() derives from DIR_LOGS, which the env's dsynth.ini pins to /work/dsynth/logs. An in-env hook enqueues to /work/dsynth/logs/evidence/queue/pending; the runner watches the host path from polytropos.conf. They never meet.

2. PUT-FS. The hook gzips the full log to ${DIR_LOGS}/evidence/full-logs/... and sends that path with put-fs. The store, on the host, writes an artifact_refs row with backend='fs' and an fs_path it cannot open. put-fs is the only artifact API that cannot cross a filesystem boundary — the runner's own writes (artifact_store_put) and reads (materialize_bundle into a tempdir) are both already HTTP.

Both are LATENT on x6: /work/dsynth/logs/evidence does not exist, because no in-chroot hook has ever completed a run. Every job in the host queue came from host-side invocations. The first successful in-env hook run trips both.

What still works today, and is worth knowing: bundle-upsert and put-blob are HTTP, so the bundle row and every artifact except the compressed full log DO reach the store from inside the chroot.

A bind-mount would hide this rather than fix it, and only because a chroot happens to share a kernel. The same two failures appear verbatim the moment a builder is a separate host.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A dsynth failure inside an env produces a job the runner actually picks up. 2. Every artifact_refs row the store writes is readable by the store. 3. Neither fix depends on the builder sharing a filesystem with the tracker.
notes:
CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-27, both halves, with a real dsynth build in the 2026Q3-editors_vim env.

Three genuine failures fired hook_pkg_failure: devel/glib20@bootstrap (patch phase, rejected DragonFly hunk), graphics/jpeg-turbo (configure), lang/rust (fetch).

QUEUE HALF. Three .job files landed in the env's chroot-path queue at /work/dsynth/logs/evidence/queue/pending/. The host runner queue (/tmp/polyverify/logs/evidence/queue/pending/) stayed empty. Measured, not inferred.

PUT-FS HALF. artifact_refs now holds three backend='fs' rows whose fs_path is /work/dsynth/logs/evidence/full-logs/<bundle>.full.log.gz — chroot paths the store cannot open. One per bundle, exactly as predicted.

WHAT WORKED ANYWAY, and it matters for scoping: everything HTTP crossed the boundary fine. All three bundles reached the store with the correct target @2026Q3, carrying real artifacts — glib20 alone has 19, including port/files/patch-gio_meson.build, the very patch that failed to apply. Only the two path-carrying outputs failed.
RECONFIRMED 2026-08-27 on a completely clean stack — DB wiped, env destroyed and recreated, 25-minute from-scratch build of 188 packages. Neither half is an artefact of accumulated state.

  env (chroot) queue/pending:  3 files
  host runner queue/pending:   0 files
  runner_status:               idle / waiting

and three artifact_refs rows with backend='fs' and fs_path under
/work/dsynth/logs/evidence/full-logs/ — chroot paths the store cannot
open, one per bundle.

Everything upstream of the runner now works: build_runs 1 opened and
closed (total_expected=188), 3 bundles at target @2026Q3, 43 artifacts,
3 distinct fingerprinted issues, 3 jobs rows delivered over HTTP, and
runs.build_run_id=1. The runner is the only thing that cannot see the
work, and only because it looks in a directory.

title: Step 31 — fold the artifact-store into the tracker (single service)
description:
The central side runs two HTTP services on one host:

- tracker (:8080, FastAPI) — reads state.db, serves bundle artifacts from
  a local artifact_root, and writes state.db directly.
- artifact-store (:8788, stdlib BaseHTTPRequestHandler) — the nominal
  "single writer", serving /v1/artifacts/{get,put,put-fs},
  /v1/bundles/upsert, /v1/jobs/transition, /v1/user-context.

They share one filesystem and one state.db file — the tracker reads
exactly what the artifact-store writes — so they already MUST co-locate.
Running them as two processes buys nothing and costs an extra port, an
extra thing to supervise, and a second network + auth surface the moment
a builder goes remote (poly-fij).

THE SINGLE-WRITER INVARIANT IS FICTION THREE WAYS OVER

Not two, as the backlog doc had it. Three processes write state.db:

- artifact-store, the nominal one;
- the tracker — 24 write statements across 14 tables: activity_log,
  build_results, build_runs, bundle_review_requests, bundles, events,
  issues, origin_skip_flags, port_status, tracker_active_env,
  user_context, user_context_history, user_context_requests,
  verify_requests. The doc called this "operator actions"; it is most of
  the tracker.
- the runner — 57 execute/commit sites across 9 tables (poly-fij).

Folding 31 makes the tracker the single central service and the single
writer PROCESS. The runner is then the only remaining direct-sqlite
writer, which poly-fij converts to HTTP.

THE SPLIT IS ALREADY COSTING US SOMETHING CONCRETE

The runner has two ways to fetch the same bytes and tries them in order:

    data = artifact_store_get(bundle_id, rel)      # :8788 /v1/artifacts/get
    if data is None:
        data = tracker_artifact_get(bundle_id, rel) # :8080 /api/bundles/.../artifacts/...

Two ports, two URL shapes, two accessors (_artifact_store_url and
_tracker_url), and a fallback chain that exists for no reason other than
there being two services. At two call sites. The fold deletes the
fallback, one accessor and one config knob.
design:
No change to the on-disk layout (artifact_root, objects/sha256/...) or to
the wire contract of the /v1/ endpoints — only the host:port they live
on. Keep the /v1/ paths verbatim to minimise client churn.

31a — mount the artifact-store endpoints on the FastAPI app.
Port /v1/artifacts/{get,put,put-fs}, /v1/bundles/upsert,
/v1/jobs/transition and /v1/user-context to FastAPI routes calling the
existing ArtifactStore class in-process. Define the blob put routes as
sync `def` so FastAPI dispatches them in its threadpool and a large
upload cannot block the async UI/event loop.

31b — repoint clients. The runner's ARTIFACT_STORE_URL and the hook's
artifact-store-client both default to the tracker URL; DPORTSV3_TRACKER_URL
becomes the single endpoint for blobs and state. Collapse
artifact_store_get / tracker_artifact_get into one function and delete the
fallback.

31c — retire the standalone service. Remove the :8788 bind,
ArtifactStoreServer, the Handler class and the artifact-store entry
point's argparse main. Keep the ArtifactStore class — it is now invoked
in-process by the FastAPI routes. The artifact-store-client stays: it is
what the dsynth hooks call, and it only changes which URL it points at.

31d — ops + permissions. The tracker process now WRITES artifact_root; it
only read it before. Confirm the service account has write permission,
drop polytropos_artifact_store from RC_SCRIPTS and the runbook, and start
one service instead of two.

INTERACTION WITH WHAT JUST LANDED

poly-7z1 made `dev-env hooks-install` write ARTIFACT_STORE_CLIENT,
POLYTROPOS_PYTHON and DPORTSV3_TRACKER_TARGET into the env's hooks conf.
31b removes one of the two URLs that conf carries; env_hook_settings and
the conf example both need updating, and OPERATOR_SETUP.md's hook section
with them.

put-fs deserves a decision here rather than later, and it is narrower
than "remote producers should use put-blob".

Everything else is already remote-safe. The runner WRITES via
artifact_store_put (HTTP, streamed bytes) and READS via a materialize
step that pulls a bundle into a tempdir when there is no on-disk dir —
"Materialize the bundle if it arrived via artifact-store", steps.py. The
bundle_dir tier in read_bundle_text is an optimisation for the colocated
case, not a dependency.

put-fs is the one exception: exactly one caller, hook_pkg_failure,
gzipping the full dsynth log and handing the store a path to open itself.
It is the only artifact API that cannot cross a filesystem boundary, and
it is called from the one place guaranteed to sit on the builder.

It is ALREADY WRONG in a dev-env, not just under poly-fij. The hook
computes ${DIR_LOGS}/evidence/full-logs/... which inside the env is
/work/dsynth/logs/..., a chroot path, and sends it to a store on the
host. That writes an artifact_refs row with backend='fs' and an fs_path
nothing outside the chroot can open. Latent only because
/work/dsynth/logs/evidence does not exist yet — no in-chroot hook has
completed a run. The first one that does trips it. See poly-7z1.

So: reject put-fs from a caller that does not demonstrably share the
store's filesystem, and have the hook fall back to put-blob for the
compressed log. Cheap now; a silently unreadable evidence row later.

SEQUENCING — NOT BLOCKED BY STEP 21

The backlog doc ordered this 21 -> 31 -> 17, on the grounds that 31a
would otherwise mean "physically relocating artifact_store.py's
still-scattered write code and re-consolidating later".

Checked, and it does not hold. ArtifactStore's writes are not scattered:
it is a cohesive class whose public methods already map almost
one-to-one onto the six endpoints — upsert_run_bundle, apply_transition,
put_blob, put_fs_ref, get_artifact, upsert_user_context. It already IS
the write surface for its half, and 31c above keeps the class rather than
relocating it. So 31a is "mount six routes onto an existing class" and
needs nothing from Step 21 (poly-39v, now rescoped and related-not-
blocking).

Before poly-fij's auth children (17c/17e). A builder should aim at one
service and one auth surface; wiring auth against two endpoints you are
about to collapse is wasted work. poly-fij's 17d (claim endpoint) does
not depend on this either and can land first.
acceptance_criteria: 1. One process, one port (:8080). :8788 retired, polytropos_artifact_store gone from the rc.d scripts. 2. The runner and the dsynth hooks reach blobs and state through one URL; the artifact_store_get -> tracker_artifact_get fallback is deleted. 3. The tracker is the only PROCESS writing state.db, leaving the runner as the sole direct-sqlite writer for poly-fij to convert. 4. The /v1/ wire contract and the on-disk artifact layout are unchanged.

title: 17e Operator auth, separate from runner tokens
description:
The manual-queue endpoints (POST /api/manual-requests/.../context, .../discard) are a human path, not a builder path. They need their own scheme — at minimum an operator password or SSO behind a reverse proxy.

Do not reuse runner tokens here. A compromised builder must not be able to discard manual work. Keeping the two surfaces separate is the whole point; sharing one token collapses the blast radius the epic exists to bound.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A valid runner token cannot reach an operator endpoint. 2. The operator surface is not publicly writable once the tracker leaves a private network.
notes: ORDERING: same as 17c — auth last while nothing is published.

title: 17c Authenticated writes from a builder
description:
Every write a builder makes carries Authorization: Bearer <token> and X-Runner-Id. The tracker validates the pair, rejects mismatches and revoked tokens with 401, and stamps the authenticated runner_id onto the row it wrote. bundles gets a runner_id column so every bundle is traceable to the host that produced it; older rows stay NULL.

Scope note: this presumes the builder writes over HTTP at all. Today the runner writes 9 tables through local sqlite (57 execute/commit sites) — activity_log, env_health_status, runner_status, runners, user_context_requests, bundles, issues, jobs, verify_requests. Converting those is Step 21's centralization work, and this bead depends on it rather than duplicating it.

put-fs cannot be authenticated into working: a remote builder has no path the tracker can open. Reject it with an explicit 400 for remote callers instead of writing an artifact_refs row nobody can read.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A forged or revoked token cannot write. 2. Every bundle names the builder that produced it. 3. put-fs from a remote builder fails loudly rather than storing an unreadable ref.
notes: ORDERING: lands after 17d/17a/17b, not before. Nothing is published yet, so the doc's 'auth first because the runner path is the larger attack surface' does not bind — that argument applies to an exposed tracker. Auth becomes load-bearing the day the tracker leaves a private network; land it before that day, not before it is useful.

title: 17b Stable runner identity + enrollment
description:
runner_id today is hostname-pid-uuid4[:8], regenerated on every process start. That is fine as a forensic tag and useless as an auth subject: a bearer token bound to it dies at the next restart. This is a CHANGE to identity, not an addition.

Persist the id (e.g. /usr/local/etc/polytropos/runner.json) and generate it once, at enroll. Enrollment: the operator runs an enroll subcommand on the builder pointing at the tracker URL, gets a one-time code, approves it on the tracker; the tracker issues a bearer token bound to the runner_id and the builder stores it 0600.

The runners table already exists but is liveness-shaped (runner_id, hostname, pid, started_at, last_heartbeat_at, stopped_at). It needs display_name, enrolled_at, token_sha256, revoked_at — an extension, not a new table.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A runner's id survives restart. 2. A revoked token stops that builder and no other. 3. The existing heartbeat keeps working against the same row.

title: 17a One tracker URL knob; retire hardcoded loopback
description:
Audit every hardcoded localhost / 127.0.0.1 / :8080 / :8788 across the runner and the hook scripts and route them through one config knob. The hooks already read ARTIFACT_STORE_URL and DPORTSV3_TRACKER_URL (note: the backlog doc calls the first DPORTS_ARTIFACT_STORE_URL, which is not its name). The runner has two separate accessors, _artifact_store_url() and _tracker_url(), which Step 31 collapses into one.

Cheap, and it is the step that tells us how much of the system still assumes loopback.
acceptance_criteria: 1. No hardcoded loopback address decides where a builder talks. 2. Pointing one variable at a remote host routes every runner and hook call there.

title: 17d Claim endpoint: dispatch from the DB, not the directory
description:
The core of the epic, and the one piece worth landing before any auth work.

POST /api/jobs/claim picks work in one transaction, stamps jobs.owner_id, transitions to CLAIMED with a lease expiry, and returns the payload. 204 when there is nothing to claim. The runner stops sweeping pending/ to decide what runs next and calls this instead.

NOT 'pick the oldest'. claim_next_job_batch coalesces siblings: every pending job sharing a dedup key (origin + flavor) is claimed together, one becomes the lead the runner processes, the rest are folded into job['sibling_bundle_ids'], and they all retire together. Expressed as a sequence of renames today, which is why each one has to tolerate racing. In SQL it is one statement over a group — easier, but it must not be dropped on the way across.

The queue directory does not go away; it stops being a queue. Nothing outside the builder has ever read a .job file (three globs, all in runner.py; steps.py only receives a path it is handed), so the files can keep being written for operator breadcrumbs. What changes is that nothing DECIDES from them.

Atomicity moves from the atomic rename into the DB. That is what makes the builder's location irrelevant — and it closes poly-7z1's chroot seam as a side effect, with a single local runner and no network involved.

Already in place: GET /api/jobs and GET /api/jobs/{job_id} (reads, no claim); jobs.owner_id (recorded, never branched on); the jobs row itself, INSERTed by lifecycle on the hook's HTTP hook_enqueued before any runner sees the file.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The runner selects work without reading pending/. 2. Sibling coalescing survives the move: same-key jobs are still claimed and retired as a group. 3. Two runners against one tracker never claim the same job. 4. A claimed job whose runner dies is reclaimable without a global sweep.
notes:
PREMISE CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE 2026-08-27. After a real in-env dsynth build, the store's jobs table held all three failures:

  state=queued, type=triage, origin, target=@2026Q3, bundle_id — for
  devel/glib20, graphics/jpeg-turbo and lang/rust

delivered entirely over HTTP from inside a chroot, via the hook's job-transition hook_enqueued. The runner could not act on any of them, purely because it looks in a directory instead of the DB. Nothing else was missing.

Also confirmed: the .job file itself is already location-independent. Its full contents are profile, target, origin, flavor, bundle_id, run_id, type, snippet_round, has_snippets — no paths at all. So the claim endpoint does not have to invent a payload; the jobs row plus that field set is the payload, and the runner materializes the bundle over HTTP already (steps.py materialize_bundle).

title: Step 17 — N builders, one tracker (remote runners + auth)
description:
Every piece of the loop assumes colocation today: the runner, the chroot,
the artifact-store and the tracker live on one host, talk over loopback,
and trust each other implicitly. That is fine for one builder. The
cost-effective shape going forward is N builders, one tracker — failures
aggregate in one place and build capacity scales horizontally.

The invariant that has to invert is stated in the code. `_apply_transition`
in runner.py:

    The filesystem queue is the source of truth for what processes next;
    the typed jobs table is the UI's read model.

Everything else in this epic is a consequence of swapping those two.

WHAT HOLDS IT TOGETHER TODAY, AND WHAT EVAPORATES

Mutual exclusion is an flock on `queue_root/runner.lock`
(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB, EXIT_RUNNER_LOCKED=3): one runner per queue directory.
Give each builder its own queue directory and that lock stops meaning
anything — it guards a local directory, not the shared work set.
`sweep_stranded_inflight` reasons that "the runner holds an exclusive
lock, so nothing in inflight/ belongs to a live runner", which is sound
only because of the flock and false the moment the work set is shared.
Mutual exclusion has to move into the claim.

RECONCILED AGAINST THE CODE — Step 17 in the backlog doc predates a lot

1. "the runner must stop opening state.db directly (lifecycle,
   verify_requests/user_context_requests polls)" understates it: 57
   execute/commit sites writing 9 tables — activity_log,
   env_health_status, runner_status, runners, user_context_requests,
   bundles, issues, jobs, verify_requests.
2. "the store has no GET for pending state rows" is stale. `GET
   /api/jobs` (state + target filters) and `GET /api/jobs/{job_id}`
   already exist. What is missing is an atomic CLAIM, not a read.
3. 17b proposes creating a `runners` table. One exists — but
   liveness-shaped (runner_id, hostname, pid, started_at,
   last_heartbeat_at, stopped_at), not enrollment-shaped. `jobs.owner_id`
   also exists, "recorded only; no code branches on it".
4. `runner_id` is ephemeral: hostname-pid-uuid4[:8], regenerated every
   process start. A bearer token bound to it dies on restart, so 17b is a
   CHANGE to identity, not an addition.
5. The hook variable is ARTIFACT_STORE_URL, not DPORTS_ARTIFACT_STORE_URL.

THREE THINGS THAT MAKE THIS CHEAPER THAN THE DOC'S ~600 LOC

1. The write half already landed by accident. `enqueue_job` sends
   `job-transition --event hook_enqueued` with the full detail block, and
   lifecycle INSERTs the jobs row on first transition. Every job already
   exists in the DB, delivered over HTTP, before any runner touches the
   file. The file is a parallel copy.
2. C2 set the precedent. `issues_needing_build` already derives
   confirm-build work from the DB instead of draining a queue. Job
   dispatch is the last file-driven entry point in the system.
3. Step 17 does not have to solve poly-s9m first. dsynth_active pgreps
   host-wide and gates the whole loop, and env resolution refuses when
   there is more than one env — both are correct behaviour when a host
   has exactly one env, so one-env-per-builder does not hit them.

   NOT a reason to skip poly-s9m. The real shape is M hosts x N envs: a
   big DragonFly box should run several envs, and that is the efficient
   use of it. The two compose — Step 17 is scheduling ACROSS builders,
   poly-s9m is scheduling WITHIN one — and a builder running N envs needs
   both. What this buys is only that they can land in either order.

WHAT THE QUEUE DIRECTORY IS ACTUALLY DOING

queue_root/{pending,inflight,done,failed} is two things at once: the
queue, and the audit trail. Only the first has to move.

Nothing outside the builder ever reads a .job file, in any topology.
There are three globs and all are in runner.py — the inflight sweep, the
